new_statements.quote: Tagom exhibits two register tones, a high tone and a low tone, which have a major role in its grammar marking (compare, e.g., ŋʊ́-lə́m ‘you (PL) saw’ with ŋʊ̀-lə̀m ‘you (PL) see’). The existence of lexical tone still needs to be checked.
new_statements.citation: Aldawi, Maha A. 2025. A first approach to Tagom verbal inflection and clausal negation strategies. In Helene Fatima Idris, Jan Junglas & Gertrud Schneider-Blum (eds.), Nuba Mountain Language Studies: Contemporary Perspectives, 71-104. Cologne: USB Monographs (open access).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: found verbatim in, extracted text page 83 = printed p. 73 (running head "Tagom verbal inflection and clausal negation 73"), lines 11-13: "Tagom exhibits two register tones, a high tone and a low tone, which have a major role in its grammar marking (compare, e.g., ŋʊ́-lə́m 'you (PL) saw' with ŋʊ̀-lə̀m 'you (PL) see'). The existence of lexical tone still needs to be checked." Same text lines 2970-2972 and in the excerpt file. Section 2 "Background information" (pp. 72-74) covers vowels, vowel alternation under TAM, tone, consonants; the word "stress" does not occur anywhere in Aldawi's chapter except inside the block quotation of Stevenson 1956-57: 49 on p. 79 ("Stress and vowel…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tagom (Tegali) is described as a two-tone register language (H/L) whose tones mark tense/aspect (present = low tones, past = high, perfect = high-low, p. 80); the author says nothing about word stress or its position. The only stress statements in the literature are Stevenson's (1956-57: 47, snippets only): the Tegali-Tagoi languages are 'predominantly stress-languages', stress 'plays a marked role in sound change and may have grammatical (probably also lexical) significance, e.g. RASHAD: ome keyak The men eat, ome keyǝk The men ate', and tone is doubted; no placement rule is given. Bashir 2025: 49 (same volume, on Tagoi) argues Stevenson noticed the pitch contrast and attributed it to stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Stevenson 1956-57: 46-47 (quoted by Bashir 2025: 43) notes lax/short vowel variants 'particularly in unstressed syllables where they are also often lost or represented by some kind of neutral vowel', and that the neutral vowel also occurs in stressed positions; Stevenson 1964 SNR 45: 86 (snippet) 'Stress is important, and the vowels in unstressed syllables tend to...'. Aldawi 2025: 79 quotes Stevenson 1956-57: 49 that 'stress and vowel change also play a part in tense-formation' but does not confirm it for Tagom.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (verb roots with pronominal prefixes; tone alternations on prefix and root); elicited words and sentences from two Khartoum-resident Tagom speakers, 2017-2023. Stevenson's contrast keyak/keyǝk is a word-level grammatical (present vs past) contrast.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand modern descriptions are of Tagom (= Gom = Rashad), the Rashad Town-Hills dialect of Tegali (Glottolog rash1248); Aldawi's Figure 1 places Tagom under the Tegali cluster together with Tegali, Umale and Kajakja. Stevenson's 1956-57 stress remark covers the whole Tegali-Tagoi (Rashad) group and its example is from RASHAD, i.e. the same variety. Nothing first-hand exists for Nuclear Tegali (nucl1243) beyond Meinhof 1916-17, which could not be opened.

sources.note: p. 73: two register tones H and L with a major grammatical role; lexical tone unchecked; stress is never mentioned for Tagom except inside a quotation of Stevenson 1956-57: 49 (p. 79: 'Stress and vowel change also play a part in tense-formation').
Consonant and vowel tables only (retroflex /ɖ/ and [ɨ, ʌ] in Tagom); nothing on tone or stress.
